catalog_quote: The S-K-N basic pattern with low tone from constriction or glottalization and high tone in its absence Leer has called “low-marked”. ... The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin. ... Another surprise is the difference between Northern and Southern Tutchone. In both the Tutchone and Dogrib-Mackenzie cases I have heard reports that there is considerable communication, in spite of the tone reversals. The tones are thus important, but not necessarily decisive, for mutual intelligibility, where other linguistic and sociological factors are favorable. ... The Southern Tutchone also shows very regular low-markedness for unsuffixed stems, with no definite exceptions. It is difficult to determine, however, whether it belongs with the assimilating languages with respect to tone development in [suffixed CVC and CV̨C stems; symbols garbled in] ... The reason for the vacillation is not clear, unless it indicated some neutralization or mid tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

PDF page numbers equal the typescript's running page numbers (extracted text and -f 56 return the '12 MICHAEL KRAUSS' and '56 MICHAEL KRAUSS' headers). All four quoted segments are present verbatim at the stated locators: (1) 'The S-K-N basic pattern with low tone from constriction or glottalization and high tone in its absence Leer has called "low-marked".' — p. 11, §3 tone map (the text); (2) 'The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutcho…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Southern Tutchone is a lexical tone language of the Athabaskan 'low-marked' type: stems that had Proto-Athabaskan constriction/glottalization carry low tone, others high (the reverse of neighbouring high-marked Northern Tutchone). The Yukon Native Language Centre materials (Ritter 1983 handout; 1984/1985 literacy workshops p. 6–7; 1994 session p. 5; YNLC 'About' page) describe four surface tones (high/plain unmarked, low, rising, mid/falling). No accessible source says anything about word stress or its position; Krauss's only remarks on stress concern toneless languages (Chasta Costa, Mattole, Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai, Pacific Coast Athabaskan), not Tutchone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Krauss notes vacillation/possible neutralization (mid tone) in suffixed stems (CVC-´ and CV̨C-´ types) in Southern Tutchone (p. 55–56); no exceptions to low-markedness in unsuffixed stems.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone in noun stems (Krauss's survey is explicitly noun-based, p. 1); YNLC descriptions concern the orthographic marking of tone on vowels in words; nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sout2957 has no dialect children. Krauss's Southern Tutchone tone data come from Ritter's 1975 fieldnotes (Ritter 1976 labels his Southern forms 'Burwash'), Tlen/Johnson's Kluane (Burwash Landing) glossary ms., McRoy 1974 and Krauss 1962; the YNLC materials cover the Aishihik, Klukshu, Kluane/Burwash, Haines Junction and Lake Laberge (Tàa'an Män) dialects, all with the same four-tone system. The tonal statement therefore holds for the language as a whole, not one dialect. Northern Tutchone (nort2941) is the tonal opposite (high-marked) and must not be conflated.

tone_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. and Victor K. Golla. 1981. Northern Athapaskan Languages. In June Helm (ed.), Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 6: Subarctic, 67-85. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution. (Glottolog ref 92852; ANLA CA961KG1981.)
tone_statements.quote: ...in others the constricted/nonconstricted contrast develops into a phonemic tone system, with constricted vowels becoming high-toned and nonconstricted vowels low-toned, or vice versa. ... Vowel constriction has developed into tone, but the system differs in the two dialects. In Northern Tutchone constricted vowels develop high tone (as in Kaska and Slavey-Hare); in Southern Tutchone, low tone (as in Tagish and Tahltan).
tone_statements.summary: Survey chapter: S. Tutchone tonal, PA constricted vowels > low tone, other syllables high (Fig. 1d legend), i.e. high vs low; N. Tutchone has the reverse. No inventory table, TBU, examples or stress.

tone_statements.citation: Ritter, John T. 1976. Kutchin and Tutchone Linguistics: Final Report of Research Activities 1974-1976. Submitted to the Ethnology Division, National Museum of Man, Ottawa. Typescript, Department of Education, Government of the Yukon Territory, Whitehorse, March 31, 1976. 37 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item KU972R1976b ('Gwich'in and Tutchone Linguistics').
tone_statements.quote: Like Kutchin, Tutchone has lost most of its stem-final consonants and has developed syllabic tone as a consequence. This tone displays a polar or "flip-flop" pattern between the Northern and Southern dialects: high tone before glottal stop in NT, low tone in ST: -té' (NT), -tà' (ST) "father"; tsé' (NT) sà' (ST) "beaver"; žédè (NT), yàdá (ST) "big dipper". This pattern runs throughout the lexicon.
